reportTitle: Indian Textile Industry - Equity Research Report
disclaimer: Prepared as a CA articleship practice exercise. Data was gathered from public secondary sources (financial news, brokerage result notes, and data aggregators) via web search; primary aggregators such as screener.in and moneycontrol.com were unreachable from the research environment, so several figures are estimates reconciled across sources rather than direct pulls. See each company's confidenceNotes for specifics. This is not investment advice and should not be relied upon for investment decisions without independent verification against company filings and a live market data source.

industry.competitiveLandscape: India remains the world's second-largest textile/garment producer and third-largest exporter (~4.6% share of global trade), but has lost relative cost competitiveness in 2026 after the US imposed a punitive 50% tariff (25% reciprocal + 25% penalty tied to Russian oil purchases) on Indian goods through much of H1 2026, versus Bangladesh and Vietnam at roughly 10-20%. This caused a reported ~28.7% YoY drop in US imports from India (OTEXA data) and diverted fast-fashion/basics orders to Bangladesh (which saw June 2026 exports to the US up 5.7% YoY) and Vietnam (H1 2026 exports up 1.7% to $22.2bn, aided by a flat 10% Section 122 surcharge after a US Supreme Court ruling struck down the harsher IEEPA tariff). A Feb 6, 2026 India-US interim trade framework cut the reciprocal tariff to 18% for textiles/apparel/made-ups, narrowing but not closing the gap with Bangladesh and Vietnam; China remains the highest-cost source due to stacked Section 301 duties on top of the 10% baseline. India's structural strengths (raw cotton base, full value chain from fibre to garment, and PLI-backed MMF/technical-textile capacity) support long-term positioning versus Bangladesh (cotton-apparel-focused, import-dependent on fabric) and Vietnam (higher-value, China-input-dependent, exposed to transshipment penalties), but near-term order flow favors Bangladesh and Vietnam until India's tariff parity holds and an EU FTA (still pending) is concluded.
industry.domesticVsExportSplit: Roughly 80:20 in favour of domestic consumption. The domestic textile & apparel market is estimated at about ₹16.66 lakh crore (~US$190 billion) in FY2025-26 (IBEF/PIB), versus FY26 (Apr'25-Feb'26) exports of textiles, apparel and handicrafts of US$32.63 billion (full-year run-rate roughly US$35-38 billion). Government targets a US$350 billion total industry size (domestic + exports) by 2030, with exports rising to US$100 billion (a ~19% CAGR ask) and domestic market to ~US$350 billion scale contribution — implying the domestic market will continue to be the larger driver of overall industry growth even as export ambitions rise.
industry.exportValueUsd: US$32.63 billion in textile, apparel and handicraft exports for FY26 (April 2025-February 2026, 11-month figure), per Ministry of Textiles/IBEF data reported August 2026; Ready-Made Garments (RMG) contributed US$15.77bn (44% share), Cotton Textiles US$10.25bn (29%), Man-Made Textiles US$5.23bn (15%). In rupee terms, textile exports (excluding handicrafts) grew 2.1% YoY to ₹3.16 lakh crore in FY26, with RMG up 2.9% to ₹1,39,349.6 crore. Government's stated target is US$100 billion in textile & apparel exports by 2030 (from a base of roughly US$35-38bn), implying a required ~19% CAGR.
industry.marketSizeUsd: India's domestic textile & apparel market is estimated at approximately US$190 billion (₹16.66 lakh crore) in FY2025-26 per IBEF/PIB data. The industry contributes about 2% of India's GDP and roughly 11% of manufacturing Gross Value Added (GVA), employs over 45 million people directly, and produces about 22,000 million garments annually. The government's stated ambition is to grow the combined domestic-plus-export industry to US$350 billion by 2030 (a 10% CAGR from the current base), positioning India as the world's second-largest textile/garment producer and third-largest exporter with a 4.6% share of global trade.
industry.rawMaterialTrends: Cotton: India set MSPs for the 2026-27 cotton season (announced end-July 2026) with Suvin ELS cotton at the highest support of ₹9,867/quintal and other varieties from ₹7,767 to ₹9,867/quintal; aggressive CCI (Cotton Corporation of India) procurement at these MSP levels has pushed open-market/mill procurement costs up even as open-market prices trade below MSP for lower grades, squeezing spinning-mill margins on quality/availability mismatches. Cotton prices were range-bound but firming through Q1 2026 (~$1,715/MT in Feb 2026) on planting-uncertainty and input-cost pressure. CCI resumes MSP-linked procurement from October 1, 2026 whenever market prices fall below notified MSP. Man-made fibres (MMF): polyester (77.5% of MMF volumes) and viscose (~16.5%) have shown mixed/firming trends through 2026, with rising crude-linked feedstock costs (PTA showing particular upstream strength) pushing polyester-chain prices higher even as MEG stayed comparatively stable; viscose has alternated between tight-supply firmness and periods of easing on weak downstream/apparel demand. Net effect: raw-material cost volatility (especially MSP-driven cotton costs) is compressing spinning/weaving margins, though CRISIL projects cotton-yarn makers' revenue to rebound 9-11% in FY27 on higher exports (12-14% export revenue growth) and better realisations (6-8% yarn price gains), with margins expected to expand 150-250bps as cotton-yarn spreads improve.
industry.growthOutlook: Government and industry bodies (Ministry of Textiles, IBEF) target a 10% CAGR for the overall textile & apparel industry through 2030, taking it from roughly US$190bn (domestic) plus ~US$35-38bn (exports) today to a combined US$350bn industry with US$100bn in exports by 2030 — the export leg implying an aggressive ~19% CAGR that looks stretched given FY26's modest 2.1% export growth and the US tariff overhang. CRISIL's more granular FY27 outlook is constructive for specific sub-segments: cotton-yarn makers' revenue is projected to rise 9-11% in FY27 as export-oriented downstream segments (RMG, home textiles) regain momentum amid easing trade disruptions, with margins expanding 150-250bps. The domestic apparel market itself is forecast at a more modest 3-4% CAGR by some market-research houses (IMARC, Expert Market Research) through the early 2030s, though other estimates citing rising middle-class incomes, e-commerce penetration and urbanization put underlying domestic consumption growth nearer 10-12%. Near-term (FY26-FY27), the sector's trajectory is unusually tariff-dependent: the swing from a 50% US tariff (H1 2026) to an 18% negotiated rate (post Feb 2026 interim deal) is the single largest variable for export-oriented listed players, with a full EU FTA still pending as a further potential upside catalyst.
keyDemandDrivers: Rising disposable incomes and an expanding middle class driving discretionary apparel spend
Rapid e-commerce and organized/omnichannel retail penetration widening access beyond metros
Urbanization and increasing fashion consciousness amplified by social media and global fashion exposure
Government-backed manufacturing push (PLI, PM MITRA parks, Make in India) expanding domestic capacity in MMF and technical textiles
Growing technical textiles demand from infrastructure, healthcare, automotive and agriculture end-uses (National Technical Textiles Mission)
Post-tariff-deal (Feb 2026, 18% US reciprocal rate) partial recovery in export order flow, and diversification toward EU, UK and non-US markets
Rising sustainable/eco-conscious apparel demand, growing at an estimated ~20% CAGR off a small base
FTAs and trade diversification efforts (UK FTA implementation, pursuit of an EU deal) opening preferential-access export channels
keyRisks: US tariff volatility: the 50% punitive tariff through H1 2026 (partly tied to India's Russian oil purchases) caused a reported ~28.7% YoY drop in US imports from India; even after the Feb 2026 cut to 18%, India remains priced 30-35% higher than Bangladesh/Vietnam on some product lines, risking permanent order diversion
Cotton price/MSP pressure: aggressive CCI procurement at high MSPs is pushing raw-material costs above what open-market/export-linked mills can absorb, squeezing spinning and weaving margins
Volatile crude-linked MMF feedstock costs (PTA, polyester chain) creating input-cost unpredictability for synthetic and blended textile producers
Intensifying competition from Bangladesh (near-zero-tariff US access under 10%) and Vietnam (10% flat Section 122 rate) for basics and fast-fashion orders
Small and micro exporters (per AEPC) are disproportionately exposed to US tariff shocks and have limited ability to absorb margin compression or diversify markets quickly

Execution risk on PM MITRA parks and PLI scheme: only a fraction of planned investment realized so far (~₹8,118 crore under PLI against a ₹10,683 crore outlay; PM MITRA parks still at DPR/approval stages for several sites) — delays could push back capacity-driven export gains
Global demand softness/buyer risk-aversion, with CITI (Confederation of Indian Textile Industry) flagging exporters balancing pricing, volumes and margins amid cautious global buyers
Currency and geopolitical risk (e.g., West Asia conflict raising freight/input costs and denting polyester-yarn volumes by 2-3%)
governmentPolicy: PLI Scheme for Textiles: ₹10,683 crore outlay over 5 years covering MMF apparel, MMF fabrics and technical textile products; as of March 31, 2026, 170 companies approved with ₹8,117.64 crore invested and 33,427 new jobs created (per Ministry of Textiles/PIB data)

PM MITRA (Mega Integrated Textile Region and Apparel) Parks: 7 greenfield parks approved across Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra, with a government outlay of ₹4,445 crore (2021-22 to 2027-28); DPRs worth ₹5,567 crore cleared for 3 parks, with Lucknow (UP) and Navsari (Gujarat) clearing PPP Appraisal Committee approval in June 2026; total investment interest received across all parks stands at ₹63,177 crore, each park expected to draw ~₹10,000 crore investment and generate ~1 lakh direct plus 2 lakh indirect jobs

RoDTEP (Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products): scheme extended through September 30, 2026 at rates/value caps in force as of March 31, 2026 (textile/apparel lines carry roughly 3-4% rates); rates were briefly cut 50% from Feb 23, 2026 before being restored to pre-cut levels effective March 23, 2026 as a cushion against the US tariff shock

National Technical Textiles Mission (NTTM): includes grants of up to ₹50 lakh each to 150 startups (announced 2025, rolling out through 2026) to spur innovation in high-performance fabrics (Kevlar, Nomex, Spandex-type materials); technical textiles market targeted to grow from ~US$29-45 billion currently toward US$123 billion by 2035 and US$309 billion by 2047

India-US Interim Trade Framework (announced Feb 6, 2026): cuts US reciprocal tariff on Indian textiles, apparel and made-ups from a punitive 50% (25% reciprocal + 25% penalty) to 18%, alongside a five-year US$500 billion Indian purchase commitment; full bilateral deal still being negotiated

Cotton MSP policy: Minimum Support Prices for FAQ cotton varieties for the 2026-27 season notified end-July 2026 (₹7,767-₹9,867/quintal depending on variety), with CCI procurement resuming October 1, 2026 whenever market prices fall below MSP
Overall industry target: Ministry of Textiles/Government of India target of US$350 billion combined industry size and US$100 billion in exports by 2030

companies.businessSummary: Vardhman Textiles Ltd, part of the Ludhiana-based Vardhman Group founded by the Oswal family, is one of India's largest vertically integrated textile companies spanning yarn (spinning), greige and processed fabrics, acrylic fibre, sewing thread and garments. It runs 18+ manufacturing units across four states (Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, etc.) with roughly 1.0-1.2 million spindles, ~670 MT/day yarn capacity, weaving capacity of ~193-220 million metres per annum (MMPA) and fabric processing capacity of ~180-206 MMPA, making it among the top 3 woven fabric manufacturers in India. Products are exported to over 75 countries (Bangladesh alone historically ~50% of yarn exports; the US is a major fabric/garment export market), alongside a large domestic sales base, giving a mixed export-domestic revenue profile weighted toward fabric/garment exports and yarn sold both domestically and abroad.
companies.segment: Yarn & spinning, woven fabric (grey and processed), with garments, acrylic fibre and sewing thread as adjacent segments
companies.recentDevelopments: FY26 (year ended March 2026) consolidated revenue was roughly flat (~10,093 Cr, -0.3% YoY) while consolidated PAT fell ~15% YoY to ~753 Cr (standalone PAT 740 Cr) on margin pressure from a weaker fabric division amid US tariff uncertainty and cotton cost volatility; Q4 FY26 PAT fell ~22% YoY to ~185-189 Cr on an EBITDA margin of ~11.8%. The Board (7 May 2026) recommended a final dividend of Rs 5/share and confirmed capitalisation of ~570 Cr of new assets in Q4, including a new technical textiles plant at Baddi (Himachal Pradesh, ~15 lakh metres/month, commercial production from 1 March 2026) and an expanded processing line at the Budhni (MP) facility (processed fabric capacity raised from ~175 to ~206 MMPA, commercial production from 7 March 2026) as part of a broader ~2,350 Cr expansion program (~2,000 Cr in spinning/weaving/technical textiles plus ~350 Cr at Budhni) announced since May 2024. The stock rallied sharply through 2025-26 (touching decade/all-time highs) after the US-India trade deal cut the US reciprocal tariff on Indian goods from 25% to 18%, easing a key overhang for exporters. Q1 FY27 (June 2026 quarter) showed a strong rebound: revenue up ~13% YoY to ~2,648 Cr, consolidated PAT up ~41-51% YoY to ~285-315 Cr, EBITDA margin expanding ~295 bps to ~19.4%, driven by full capacity utilisation and favourable trading gains in spinning, even as the fabric division stayed muted on delayed US orders (management expects recovery within 2-3 months).
companies.keyRisks: High dependence on volatile cotton prices (India's MSP-driven cotton is often priced above landed cost of Vietnamese/Indonesian cotton, squeezing spinning margins) combined with monsoon/crop-yield risk given India supplies ~25% of global cotton. Significant exposure to US and Bangladesh export markets creates geopolitical/tariff risk (US reciprocal tariffs on Indian textiles, and Bangladesh transit/logistics disruptions affecting ~50% of yarn exports historically) plus intense low-cost competition from Bangladesh, Vietnam, China and other South/Southeast Asian producers amid chronic sector overcapacity in yarn and greige fabric that periodically triggers price wars. Returns metrics (ROE ~7-9%, ROCE ~8-10%) have trended down from historical mid-teens levels, and large ongoing capex (~2,350 Cr program) carries execution and ramp-up/utilisation risk for the new Baddi and Budhni capacities.
companies.dataAsOf: CMP/market cap/P/E as of 5-11 August 2026; 52-week range and shareholding as of Q3 FY26 (Dec 2025) / Aug 2026; financial results (revenue, PAT, margins, ROE, ROCE) for FY2025-26 (year ended 31 March 2026), reported May 2026

Debt-to-equity (0.10), ROE (8.29%) and ROCE (8.86%) are approximate consensus values pieced together from conflicting snippets (sources showed ROE ranging 7.0%-8.93% and ROCE ranging 8.14%-9.9% across different quarters/TTM windows) — treat as indicative, not precise. 3-year sales and profit CAGR could not be reliably sourced (only a "poor 5-year sales growth of ~9.96%" and a "-5% 1-year revenue CAGR, -14% EBITDA CAGR" figure for FY24 were found, which are not the requested 3-year metric) — set to null per instructions rather than guessed. Revenue/PAT figures mix consolidated (10,092.53 Cr revenue / 753.20 Cr PAT) and standalone (9,652.33 Cr revenue / 740.02 Cr PAT) reporting across sources; consolidated figures were used as the primary numbers. Given the CA-articleship context, Jaimin should treat these as a solid first-pass dataset to be verified against the FY25-26 Annual Report / screener.in (accessed directly, outside this blocked environment) before use in a client-facing peer comparison report.

companies.businessSummary: Trident Ltd is the flagship company of the Trident Group (Punjab-based, founder-promoter Rajinder Gupta), a vertically integrated textile and paper manufacturer. It makes cotton yarn, terry towels/bath linen, bed linen, and wheat-straw-based paper, with plants concentrated at Barnala (Punjab) and Budni (Madhya Pradesh). As of March 31, 2026 installed capacity was ~7.97 lakh spindles (yarn), 90,000 MTPA bath linen, 63.87 million metres bed linen, and 1,75,000 MTPA paper — it markets itself as having the world's largest single-location terry towel manufacturing capacity. Exports account for roughly 52-53% of revenue (150+ countries, chiefly US and EU), while the legacy yarn business still contributes about a third of overall revenue.
companies.segment: Home textiles (terry towel & bed linen) and Yarn, plus a Paper (wheat-straw based) segment
companies.dataAsOf: Market data (CMP/market cap/P/E/52-week range) as of ~18 August 2026; financials are for FY2025-26 (year ended 31 March 2026), the latest full fiscal year reported
companies.recentDevelopments: FY26 full-year (ended Mar-2026) consolidated revenue was ~₹6,775 Cr (down ~4% YoY) with net profit of ~₹377 Cr (up ~2% YoY); EBITDA slipped to ₹951 Cr from ₹971 Cr in FY25 and net debt rose to ₹975 Cr from ₹895 Cr as capex ramped up. Quarter-to-quarter the year was volatile: Q1 FY26 (Jun-2025) saw a sharp YoY profit jump on strong yarn-segment performance and optimism around the India-UK FTA; Q3 FY26 (Dec-2025) saw margin pressure as raw-material costs rose ~18% even as yarn revenue surged; Q4 FY26 (Mar-2026) profit rebounded sharply sequentially even as revenue stayed soft YoY. An interim dividend of ₹0.50/share was paid during the year. In November 2025 the company announced a ₹2,000 Cr expansion in Punjab — ₹1,500 Cr at Barnala to scale up terry-towel capacity and modernize the paper unit, plus ₹500 Cr for a new Mohali corporate office/capability centre — layered on an earlier ₹1,000 Cr sustainability/modernization capex plan unveiled at Bharat Tex 2025, all framed around a stated ambition of roughly 3x growth by 2027. Management has cited India's ~18% negotiated US tariff on home-textile exports (versus ~19-20% for Bangladesh/Vietnam) as a relative competitive opening being used to justify the capacity build-out.
companies.keyRisks: (1) Heavy export dependence (~52-53% of revenue, concentrated in the US and EU) leaves earnings exposed to US tariff/trade-policy shifts — the Section 122 tariff regime and reciprocal-tariff litigation remain unsettled, and margins are already described as "wafer-thin" for Indian exporters. (2) Raw-material price volatility — cotton for yarn/textiles and pulp/wheat-straw for paper — has repeatedly compressed operating margins (e.g., raw-material costs up ~18% in a recent quarter). (3) The yarn business (~34% of revenue) is commodity-like and highly cyclical, producing lumpy quarter-to-quarter profit swings and a negative reported 3-year profit CAGR (likely reflecting a high FY22 cotton-price-boom base rather than a structural decline). (4) Rising debt and execution risk around the newly announced ₹2,000 Cr Punjab capex amid already-thin ROE/ROCE (~9-11%). (5) INR/USD currency exposure given the large export book.
companies.confidenceNotes: Figures were cross-checked across multiple secondary aggregators since direct screener.in access was blocked by the network proxy (relied on search-engine snippets of screener.in instead of the live page). CMP (₹24.94), market cap (₹12,652 Cr) and P/E (33.55) are internally consistent (implied shares outstanding ~507 Cr and implied net profit ~₹377 Cr match the reported FY26 PAT), giving reasonably high confidence in that cluster. Some figures showed genuine spread across sources and should be treated as approximate: 52-week high was reported as both ₹30.94 and ₹33.66 depending on source/date — used the figure paired with the same CMP/mcap dataset; dividend yield ranged 1.48%-2.03% across sources; P/B ranged 2.62-2.90; TTM/annual net profit was reported variously as ₹370-404 Cr depending on the exact trailing window used (FY24 ~₹350 Cr, FY25 ~₹370 Cr, FY26 ~₹377 Cr, one TTM cut ~₹395-404 Cr) — I used the officially announced FY26 (Apr'25-Mar'26) full-year figure of ₹377 Cr net profit / ₹6,775 Cr revenue as the primary "latest full fiscal year" figures. One search result (freepressjournal, Q3 FY26) reported quarterly revenue of "₹15,745 Cr" and 9-month revenue of "₹50,685 Cr" — these are almost certainly a decimal/unit error (roughly 10x too high given full-year revenue is only ₹6,775 Cr) and were NOT used; I relied instead on the full-year Q4/FY26 result announcements (equitybulls/investywise) which are internally consistent. ROE (9.61%), ROCE (10.73%) and debt-to-equity (0.22) came from a single aggregator (search-snippet, likely trendlyne/tijori-derived) and are broadly consistent with net-debt (₹975 Cr) versus an implied equity base (~₹4,300-4,800 Cr from market-cap/P-B), but were not independently verified against a primary filing. 3-year sales CAGR (8.19%) and especially 3-year profit CAGR (-23.36%) should be treated cautiously — the negative profit CAGR likely reflects an elevated FY22/23 cotton-price-boom base year rather than an ongoing decline, since FY24→FY26 profits were roughly flat-to-slightly-up. No paid/subscription sources or company filings (BSE/NSE XBRL, annual report) were opened directly; all data is from public news/aggregator search snippets.

companies.segment: Home textiles (terry towels, bed & bath linen) with a growing flooring (carpets/rugs) segment
companies.businessSummary: Welspun Living Ltd, part of the Welspun Group, is one of the world's largest home-textile manufacturers, making terry towels, bed & bath linen, and other home textile products, plus a flooring/carpets & rugs business. Manufacturing is concentrated at Anjar (Gujarat, hub for bed sheets and terry towels), Vapi (Gujarat, terry towels and rugs), and a Telangana facility for advanced textiles and flooring; installed cotton terry-towel capacity is about 23,500 MTPA. The company is historically export-heavy, with roughly 60% of revenue from outside India and the US alone historically accounting for ~59-65% of sales, though management is now explicitly pursuing diversification toward domestic India and non-US markets (targeting non-US revenue above 50%, versus ~41% currently). Home textiles is the dominant segment (~90%+ of revenue), with flooring a smaller (~8-10%) but faster-growing contributor.
companies.recentDevelopments: FY2025-26 was a sharply weaker year: consolidated revenue fell to ₹9,399 crore from ₹10,545 crore in FY25 (-11%), and PAT collapsed to ₹212.89 crore from ₹644 crore (-67%), driven by US tariff escalation (rates swung from ~10% to as high as 50% and back down during 2025-26), cautious US customer ordering, and West Asia-related disruption. Q2 FY26 (Sep-25 qtr) was the trough: revenue -16.4% YoY to ₹2,456 crore and PAT crashed 93% to ₹13 crore on a 6.8% EBITDA margin. Q3 FY26 (Dec-25 qtr) saw revenue still down ~10% YoY but EBITDA margin recovering to 7.7%, with management citing new India-US and India-EU trade agreements as a structural positive for India's sourcing competitiveness. Q4 FY26 (Mar-26 qtr) revenue was ₹2,435 crore (-8% YoY, +7.7% QoQ) with PAT of ~₹104 crore; the board approved a ₹252 crore buyback (1.44 crore shares at ₹175/share), settled and shares extinguished in June 2026. The turnaround became visible in Q1 FY2026-27 (Jun-26 qtr, reported 13-Aug-2026): revenue jumped ~24% YoY to ~₹2,795-2,828 crore and PAT rose ~83-84% YoY to ~₹161 crore, with EBITDA margin expanding to ~12.5% on volume recovery, better mix, and cost actions; home textiles grew ~26% YoY and flooring ~7% YoY. The stock hit a fresh 52-week high (~₹182.8-182.9) on 18-Aug-2026 following this print. Capex for FY26 was ~₹472 crore, with ₹400-500 crore guided for FY27, largely for automation, modernisation and debottlenecking (including an Anjar facility modernisation program).
companies.keyRisks: Heavy revenue concentration in exports and specifically the US market (historically ~60-65% of sales) leaves earnings highly exposed to US tariff policy swings and order deferrals/inventory corrections by large US retail customers, as starkly illustrated by the FY26 profit collapse and subsequent Q1 FY27 rebound. Raw material cost volatility (cotton prices and crude-linked synthetic fibre costs both rose materially during FY26) creates ongoing margin uncertainty. Quarterly earnings have shown extreme swings within FY26 (a >90% profit decline in one quarter followed by an 84% YoY jump two quarters later), indicating limited near-term earnings visibility and high operating leverage against a large fixed-cost/capex base. Geopolitical and logistics disruption (West Asia conflict was cited as an FY26 headwind) and currency/freight volatility add further risk given the export-oriented model.
companies.dataAsOf: Market data (CMP, market cap, P/E, 52-week range) as of approximately 19-20 August 2026; financial metrics are FY2025-26 (year ended 31-Mar-2026) annual results announced 15-May-2026, with the most recent quarter being Q1 FY2026-27 (Apr-Jun 2026) reported 13-Aug-2026; shareholding pattern as of the June 2026 quarter.
companies.confidenceNotes: screener.in, moneycontrol.com, and tickertape.in were all blocked by the network egress proxy in this environment, so figures were triangulated from web search snippets and secondary aggregators (business-standard, marketsmojo, univest, moneyworks4me, simplywall.st-derived search results, scanx.trade, investywise) rather than fetched directly from a single primary source — cross-check against screener.in/moneycontrol is recommended before using in a formal report. ROE/ROCE in particular vary widely by source (search results returned figures from ~4.5% to ~13.8% depending on whether the period was FY26-only, TTM, or a 3-year average) because FY26 profit collapsed to ₹213 crore from ₹644 crore in FY25 before rebounding sharply in Q1 FY27; the 4.51%/5.8% figures used here are the FY26 full-year figures and understate the company's more normal ~11-13% run-rate ROE/ROCE seen in FY24-25 and implied by the Q1 FY27 recovery. Debt-to-equity (0.68) and market cap/P/E carry similar cross-source variance (market cap was seen quoted anywhere from ~₹13,300 crore in May 2026 to ~₹17,050 crore in August 2026, partly reflecting the ₹252 crore/1.44 crore-share buyback completed in June 2026 which changed the share count) — treat as approximate. Dividend yield (0.95%) is computed from the last declared dividend of ₹1.70/share (record date 27-Jun-2025, paid Oct-2025) against the current CMP; it does not capture the additional capital returned via the FY26 buyback. 3-year profit CAGR (~1.6%) is heavily depressed by the FY26 tariff-driven earnings collapse (FY23 PAT ₹203cr vs FY26 PAT ₹213cr) and should be read alongside the sharp Q1 FY27 earnings recovery rather than as a steady trend. Export/domestic revenue split figures came from slightly inconsistent secondary reporting (ranging ~59-65% US/export dependence) and should be verified against the company's own investor presentation for precision.

companies.businessSummary: Raymond Lifestyle Ltd (RLL) is India's leading branded textile and apparel company, demerged from Raymond Ltd and listed separately on NSE/BSE in September 2024. It holds the largest market share in India's worsted suiting fabric industry and owns brands Raymond, Park Avenue, ColorPlus, Parx, Raymond Ready-to-Wear and Ethnix. Fabric manufacturing is spread across Vapi (Gujarat), Chhindwara (MP) and Jalgaon (Maharashtra) plants with combined worsted suiting capacity of ~43 million metres, plus a Kolhapur (Maharashtra) high-value cotton/linen shirting plant with ~26 million metre capacity. Its export-oriented Garmenting business (white-labelled manufacturing via subsidiaries Silver Spark Apparel, EverBlue Apparel and Celebrations Apparel) runs four plants in Bengaluru with combined annual capacity of ~2.2 million tailored jackets, 2.4 million trousers and 2.4 million shirts, plus a new Ethiopia plant (2.6 million pieces/year) being commissioned for duty-free access to the US and Europe. RLL exports to 45+ countries; the Garmenting segment's export mix has historically been ~60-65% US, ~10% UK and ~5-8% Europe, and the company is actively shifting toward a larger Europe share amid US tariff volatility. Revenue mix is dominated by the domestic Branded Textile and Branded Apparel businesses, supplemented by the largely export-facing Garmenting and High-Value Cotton Shirting segments.
companies.segment: Branded apparel & fabric (menswear) with export garment manufacturing
companies.recentDevelopments: Q3 FY26 (Oct-Dec 2025): record quarterly revenue of ₹1,883 Cr (+5% YoY), EBITDA +23% to ₹271 Cr (margin 14.4%), but PAT fell ~33-43% YoY (reports vary, ~₹43-64 Cr) as the Garmenting/export segment revenue fell ~17% to ₹258 Cr on US tariff pressure, even as Branded Textile (₹951 Cr, EBITDA margin 21.8%) and Branded Apparel (₹482 Cr) grew. Q4 FY26 (Jan-Mar 2026): full-year Total Income crossed ₹7,000 Cr for the first time (₹7,034 Cr, +11% YoY) and FY26 EBITDA rose 23% to ₹804 Cr (margin 11.4%, up from 10.2%), but the quarter itself posted a consolidated net loss of ₹52.06 Cr on exceptional charges, apparel-business pressure and inventory hits; Garmenting revenue rebounded 38% YoY to ₹342 Cr post the US-India trade deal. The Board declared a ₹1/share final dividend and management called out FY27 as a "Year of Consolidation" focused on operating optimization, premiumization and casualization in Branded Apparel. companies.businessSummary: K.P.R. Mill Ltd (KPR Mill), headquartered in Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, is one of India's largest vertically integrated textile-to-apparel manufacturers and garment exporters. Operations span cotton/viscose yarn spinning (~3.7 lakh spindles; ~1,00,000 MT cotton yarn + 4,000 MT viscose yarn p.a.), knitted fabric processing (~40,000 MT p.a.), and readymade knitted-garment manufacturing (~157 million pieces p.a. capacity across ~15 units). It also runs a diversified sugar and green-energy arm — a 20,000 TCD sugar mill, a 360 KLPD ethanol distillery, a 90 MW multi-fuel cogeneration plant, and 66 windmills (~62 MW). Garments are almost entirely export-oriented (sold to ~60 global brands including Primark, Walmart, H&M, M&S, ASDA and Kmart, with Europe ~60% and North America ~20% of exports), while yarn, fabric and sugar are sold mainly in the domestic market, giving the group roughly a 35-40% export / 60-65% domestic overall revenue mix.

companies.businessSummary: Page Industries Ltd is the exclusive licensee of JOCKEY International Inc. for manufacturing, marketing and distribution of the JOCKEY innerwear/athleisure brand across India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Maldives, Oman, Qatar and the UAE, and is also the exclusive licensee of Speedo International for India. It designs, makes and sells men's, women's and kids' innerwear, leisurewear, activewear and swimwear through exclusive brand outlets, large-format/multi-brand retail and e-commerce. Manufacturing is spread across 15+ owned units, historically concentrated around Bengaluru/Mysuru/KR Pete in Karnataka, plus a newly inaugurated ~₹750-crore, 650,000 sq.ft. facility at Cuttack (Ramdaspur), Odisha (men's innerwear, socks, elastics) with a second ~₹250-crore Odisha unit (Bhuinpur, Khurda) under construction; total installed capacity is roughly 280 million pieces/annum. The business is overwhelmingly domestic (India)-focused — the company has largely stopped disclosing a precise export/international revenue split in recent years, but international sales under the Jockey license extension to neighbouring countries are understood to be a small, single-digit percentage of total revenue.

The rapid shift toward quick-commerce/e-commerce is pushing the company toward an "outright sale" model that reduces its control over retail pricing and consumer experience. The stock also carries a rich valuation (P/E ~56x, P/B in the high-20s/30s) after falling roughly 23% from its 52-week high, leaving limited room for execution misses, and faces intensifying competition from established innerwear players (Lux, Rupa, VIP Clothing, Amante) and newer D2C athleisure/innerwear brands.

companies.businessSummary: Gokaldas Exports Ltd, established 1979 and headquartered in Bengaluru, is one of India's largest apparel manufacturers and exporters, supplying woven and knit garments to global brands/retailers such as Walmart, Gap and JCPenney. It runs 25+ manufacturing units across India plus two recently acquired international platforms — Atraco Group (4 units in Kenya, 1 in Ethiopia; acquired Jan 2024 for ~$55 million) and Matrix Design & Industries (4 knitwear units in Gurugram, Haryana, 1 in Ranchi, Jharkhand; acquired FY24 for an enterprise value of ~₹489 crore) — taking combined group output to roughly 90 million garments a year. The business is overwhelmingly export-oriented: the US alone accounts for roughly 75% of standalone sales, with the UK, France and Canada as other key destinations, though the company is now actively pushing into Europe and Africa to diversify away from US tariff exposure.
companies.recentDevelopments: FY25 (ended Mar 2025) saw record consolidated revenue of ~₹3,864-3,917 crore, up ~63% YoY, mainly from full-year consolidation of the Atraco and Matrix acquisitions, with PAT of ₹158.54 crore. In FY26 (ended Mar 2026) revenue growth moderated to ~3-4% (₹3,988-4,065 crore per different reporting lines) while PAT fell ~37% to ₹100.13 crore, as newly-imposed US tariffs on Indian apparel forced the company to absorb/discount over ₹90 crore in tariff-related costs to retain customers — PAT plunged ~71% YoY in both Q2 FY26 and Q3 FY26. A sequential recovery followed: Q4 FY26 PAT of ₹35.96 crore (+146% QoQ, still -32% YoY) and then Q1 FY27 (June 2026 quarter, reported ~12 Aug 2026) PAT of ₹44.3 crore (+6.8% YoY) on revenue of ₹1,153.5 crore (+20.7% YoY), suggesting margin pressure is easing. Capacity expansion has continued through the downturn: a new sewing factory in Bhopal, MP (Phase I: 3 million pieces/year, Phase II to double it), a new knits-processing facility in Perundurai, Tamil Nadu, and an additional leased woven/knit unit in Bommanahalli, Bengaluru. Management commentary has centered on diversifying export markets toward Europe and Africa to reduce US tariff risk.
companies.keyRisks: (1) Heavy customer/geography concentration — roughly 75% of sales tied to the US market and a handful of large global retail customers, leaving revenue exposed to US trade policy (tariffs) and customer-specific demand cycles, as demonstrated by the FY26 profit collapse. (2) Margin volatility around the Atraco/Matrix integration and tariff pass-through — EBITDA/PAT swung sharply through FY26 (PAT down ~71% YoY in two separate quarters) and leverage has risen (debt-to-EBITDA reported near ~2.17x, long-term debt increasing), adding financial risk if the earnings recovery stalls. (3) Thin promoter base and near-zero dividend — promoter holding is only ~9% following Blackstone's 2017 exit (control now via Mathew Cyriac/Florintree entities), and the company has paid almost no dividend since 2023, plus it carries the sector's usual exposure to cotton/yarn input costs, labour cost inflation, and currency movements.
